newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Heavy fighting rocks Cambodian capital.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting rocks Cambodian capital.

text.p: Heavy fighting rocked the Cambodian capital on Sunday as forces loyal to the rival prime ministers battled for a second day and thousands of people fled the city.
Smoke billowed over the city centre where shells were falling. Explosions were heard near the palace and government buildings.
The fighting, which started on Saturday, resumed at dawn. First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh accused his former battlefield enemy, Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, of attempting a coup.
Ranariddh, currently in France on what was described as a private visit, issued a statement there describing the actions against his forces as a coup.
"We consider that what is currently happening in Phnom Penh is a coup d'etat perpetuated by Mr Hun Sen," said a statement issued in Paris in the name of Ranariddh.
But a radio station controlled by powerful Hun Sen denied on Sunday that a coup was under way. The radio urged people to remain calm, and said government troops were fighting Khmer Rouge guerrillas.

"It is not a coup. If it were a coup FUNCINPEC ministers and officials would be arrested," the radio said, referring to Ranariddh's royalist party. "The government would like to appeal to the people to remain calm," the radio said. "The government is fighting with Khmer Rouge and the Khmer Rouge are shelling Phnom Penh like they did in 1975," the radio said, referring to the Maoist guerrillas' victory over a U.S.-backed government in April 1975.

The Vietnamese Foreign Ministry on Saturday said Hun Sen was in Vietnam on holiday. But a Cambodian diplomat in Hanoi said on Sunday the second prime minister was definitely not in Hanoi and was believed to have returned to Cambodia.
King Sihanouk, Ranariddh's father, was believed to be in Beijing undergoing medical treatment.
Thousands of people, heavily laden with belongings, were seen streaming out of the western part of the city where the fighting was taking place while many others were piling into cars and trucks.

Sustained shelling began just before dawn and continued into the morning. The fighting appeared to be in the area of a well-fortified compound where top generals and officials loyal to Ranariddh live.

Ranariddh's top military commander, General Nhiek Bun Chhay, denied rumours that he had surrendered. "No surrender, the situation's getting more and more tense," the general, who was holed up at his main military base near Phnom Penh airport, told Reuters by mobile telephone.

Shells occasionally landed in the city centre, where short bursts of automatic weapons fire could also be heard. A huge cloud of black smoke rose from the area of the city where the fighting was taking place, apparently from a burning petrol station. Several houses in the area were also on fire, witnesses said.
Residents in the capital said prices in markets, which opened briefly on Sunday morning, had doubled overnight.
"The markets were fairly busy early this morning with people buying food, but the stalls are dead right now," said a photographer. "A lot of people are streaming out of the area of the fighting."

Military officials said casualty figures were not known, but at least four people were killed and 20 wounded on Saturday, hospital sources said. The Cambodian Red Cross said on Sunday there were 52 casualties but gave no breakdown on the number of dead or wounded.

Troops loyal to Hun Sen, who outnumber forces loyal to Ranariddh in the capital, were stationed on city streets. At least one tank was seen near Ranariddh's official residence and an armoured car was parked outside the Royal Palace.

The road to the airport was closed. Major airlines that normally fly into Phnom Penh announced cancellations of flights there on Saturday and several said they would also scrap scheduled flights on Sunday.
The fighting erupted on Saturday after Hun Sen ordered a crackdown against "illegal troops" being brought into the capital under Ranariddh's command.
Hun Sen said the prince was bringing Khmer Rouge defectors into the city to bolster his troop strength. Ranariddh denied the accusation.
The two prime ministers head a fractured coalition government foremed after a United Nations-run election in 1993.

A bitter row over power sharing has been inflamed in recent weeks after Ranariddh said he was negotiating peace with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla groups and might strike a deal with the rebels if they borke with hated leader Pol Pot and recognised the constitution.
Nominal Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Samphan announced on Sunday that he supported the constitution and said Pol Pot's regime had ended.
